Spectral libraries

Source: vignettes/library.Rmd
library.Rmd

A spectral library says, for each precursor (a peptide or proteoform at one charge), where a search should expect to find it: its m/z, its retention time, its ion mobility, and the fragment ions its MS2 spectrum should hold, with their relative intensities. MetaMorpheus and mzLib write libraries in mzLib’s binary .msl format, predicted (Prosit, through Koina) or built from a search. mzLibR reads them with mzLib’s own reader, so a library reads in R exactly as MetaMorpheus reads it.

question function mzLib
what precursors does this library hold? library_read() MslFileTypeHandler.Open, MslLibrary.GetEntry
is this retention time iRT or minutes? the retention_time_unit column MslLibraryEntry.RtIsCalibrated
how many targets, decoys and entrapment precursors? the decoy_contaminant_target column DecoyContaminantTargetLabel.For
what are a precursor’s fragment ions? library_read(fragments = TRUE) MslFragmentIon
can I read a library too large for memory? library_read(index_only_threshold = ) MslLibrary.LoadIndexOnly
several libraries into one table library_read_many() the same reader, in one bridge process

Two small libraries are used. myPrositLib.msl is mzLib’s own test library myPrositLib.msp (five Prosit-predicted precursors) converted to .msl by mzLib. synthetic_library.msl holds six precursors written to cover every field: a target, its decoy, an entrapment target whose retention time is in minutes, an entrapment decoy, a predicted precursor with nothing measured, and a proteoform. Both are in pyMzLib’s pkg/python/tests/fixtures/library/.

Every precursor 

lib <- library_read("synthetic_library.msl")
lib
#> <mzlibr_library_records> E:\CodeReview\wt-py-library-read\pkg\python\tests\fixtures\library\synthetic_library.msl: 6 precursors (4 target, 2 decoy), .msl format 3
#>   precursor m/z 406.242 to 952.493
#>   6 precursor(s) returned
#>   ! retention_time is in iRT and minutes: read retention_time_unit on each row
c(lib$record_count, lib$target_count, lib$decoy_count, lib$proteoform_count)
#> [1] 6 4 2 1
lib$records[, c("precursor_index", "full_sequence", "charge_state", "precursor_mz",
                "decoy_contaminant_target")]
#>   precursor_index     full_sequence charge_state precursor_mz
#> 1               1          PEPTIDEK            2     465.7400
#> 2               2          KEDITPEP            2     465.7401
#> 3               3          PEPTLDEK            2     458.7462
#> 4               4          KEDLTPEP            2     458.7463
#> 5               5       ELVISLIVESK            3     406.2420
#> 6               6 MAHVRSGKHQIPAEALQ            2     952.4930
#>   decoy_contaminant_target
#> 1                        T
#> 2                        D
#> 3                       ET
#> 4                       ED
#> 5                        T
#> 6                        T

One row per precursor, in the library’s stored order. precursor_index is the position in the file, 1-based in R as every position is (mzLib’s MslLibrary.GetEntry takes it from 0). It is not m/z order: mzLib’s own GetAllEntries enumerates by ascending m/z, so sort on precursor_mz if that is the order you want.

What each column is

The names are mzLib’s MslLibraryEntry properties. Where mzLib stores a value it documents as “not available”, the column holds NA:

column what it is NA means
precursor_index position in the library, 1-based never NA
full_sequence, base_sequence mzLib bracket notation, e.g. PEPTM[Common Variable:Oxidation on M]IDE; the bare residues never NA
precursor_mz precursor m/z, (M + zH)/z never NA
charge_state precursor charge never NA
retention_time, retention_time_unit the time, and whether it is "iRT" or "minutes" never NA
ion_mobility 1/K0, in V s/cm2 mzLib stored 0.0, “not available”
is_decoy, is_entrapment, decoy_contaminant_target target, decoy and entrapment flags, and mzLib’s label T, D, ET or ED never NA
protein_accession, protein_name, gene_name the source protein mzLib stored an empty string: no protein
is_proteotypic the library writer’s proteotypic flag never NA
q_value the library’s q-value for the precursor mzLib stored NaN: no q-value, as in a predicted library
elution_group_id shared by every precursor of one base sequence never NA
molecule_type Peptide, Proteoform, Oligonucleotide or Glycopeptide never NA
source_type Predicted, Empirical, or EmpiricalRefined (predicted intensities, measured time or mobility) never NA
dissociation_type e.g. HCD; Unknown when the library does not say never NA
nce normalized collision energy, a whole number mzLib stored 0: unknown

The empirical target shows the values filled in, and the predicted precursor shows them “not available”:

lib$records[c(1, 5), c("ion_mobility", "q_value", "nce", "protein_accession", "source_type")]
#>   ion_mobility q_value nce protein_accession source_type
#> 1         0.95   0.001  28            P02768   Empirical
#> 5           NA      NA  NA              <NA>   Predicted

A whole column can have no source at all. myPrositLib.msl has no protein table and no ion mobility, so those columns are named in absent_fields and are NA in every row:

prosit <- library_read("myPrositLib.msl")
prosit$absent_fields
#> [1] "ion_mobility"      "protein_accession" "protein_name"     
#> [4] "gene_name"
prosit$records$nce
#> [1] NA NA NA NA NA
prosit$records$dissociation_type[[1]]
#> [1] "Unknown"

The .msp it was converted from records Collision_energy=30.0, yet nce is NA. That is not a reading error. mzLib converts a text library through LibrarySpectrum, which has no field for NCE, dissociation type, q-value, ion mobility or protein, so MslLibraryEntry.FromLibrarySpectrum writes mzLib’s “not available” value for each. A converted library has none of them.

Retention time: iRT or minutes, row by row

A library stores each precursor’s retention time either as an indexed retention time (iRT, a unitless scale anchored on reference peptides) or as minutes in one particular run. Which one is a flag on each precursor (MslLibraryEntry.RtIsCalibrated), and one library can hold both. So the unit is a column, not a property of the file:

lib$records[1:4, c("full_sequence", "retention_time", "retention_time_unit")]
#>   full_sequence retention_time retention_time_unit
#> 1      PEPTIDEK           35.2                 iRT
#> 2      KEDITPEP           35.2                 iRT
#> 3      PEPTLDEK           21.4             minutes
#> 4      KEDLTPEP           33.0                 iRT

Never plot or compare retention_time without retention_time_unit. mzLibR converts nothing: iRT becomes minutes only through a calibration against a run, which is not in the library. Keep the rows of one unit before you use the numbers:

irt <- lib$records[lib$records$retention_time_unit == "iRT", ]
c(irt = nrow(irt), all = nrow(lib$records))
#> irt all 
#>   5   6

iRT can be negative; Prosit predicts -15.77 for one of the myPrositLib.msl precursors. A retention_time of exactly 0 deserves suspicion: mzLib’s conversion from a text library writes 0 when the spectrum had no retention time, and documents no sentinel for it, so 0 is passed through as a value.

Targets, decoys and entrapment

The library is unfiltered. Decoys and entrapment precursors are rows like any other. decoy_contaminant_target is mzLib’s own label, written by DecoyContaminantTargetLabel.For: T target, D decoy, ET entrapment target, ED entrapment decoy. The .msl format has no contaminant flag, so C never appears.

table(lib$records$decoy_contaminant_target)
#> 
#>  D ED ET  T 
#>  1  1  1  3
lib$records$full_sequence[!lib$records$is_decoy]
#> [1] "PEPTIDEK"          "PEPTLDEK"          "ELVISLIVESK"      
#> [4] "MAHVRSGKHQIPAEALQ"

Entrapment is a target for the search: it competes with the real targets, so target_count includes the entrapment targets and decoy_count the entrapment decoys. To count only the real targets, keep decoy_contaminant_target == "T".

Fragment ions

With fragments = TRUE the table is one row per fragment ion, the precursor’s columns repeated on each row, then the fragment’s own. limit and offset still count precursors:

ions <- library_read("synthetic_library.msl", fragments = TRUE, limit = 1)
c(precursors = ions$returned_count, rows = ions$row_count)
#> precursors       rows 
#>          1          6
ions$records[, c("annotation", "fragment_mz", "fragment_intensity", "residue_position", "neutral_loss")]
#>   annotation fragment_mz fragment_intensity residue_position neutral_loss
#> 1         y1    147.1128               0.40                8      0.00000
#> 2         b2    227.1026               0.30                2      0.00000
#> 3         y2    276.1554               1.00                7      0.00000
#> 4   bIy[2-5]    326.1710               0.10                2      0.00000
#> 5 y3-18.0106    373.2082               0.20                6    -18.01056
#> 6 y4-43.0058    461.2242               0.15               NA    -43.00581

What the numbers are:

  • fragment_intensity is relative within its precursor, 0 to 1. mzLib’s writer scales each precursor’s most intense fragment to 1, so intensities are comparable within a precursor and not across precursors.
  • neutral_loss is in Da, negative for a loss, and 0 means no loss. It is 0, not NA, because 0 Da is the value of “no loss”, so fragment_mz and neutral_loss stay usable together.
  • annotation is mzLib’s library rendering (MslFragmentIon.Annotation): the loss signed to four decimals and, for a charge above 1, the charge appended (y4^2+). It differs from Product.Annotation elsewhere in mzLib, so do not match the two strings against each other.
  • An internal ion (bIy[2-5]) has is_internal TRUE, its C-terminal type in secondary_product_type and its end residue in secondary_fragment_number. Both are NA on terminal ions.
  • residue_position is NA for a fragment with a custom neutral loss, like the -43.0058 above. The .msl format reuses that field to index its table of custom losses, and mzLib reads it back as 0. The loss itself survives. Named losses (water, ammonia, phosphate) keep their position.
  • fragment_count on each row is how many fragment ions the precursor has. A precursor with none is still one row, with fragment_count 0 and every fragment cell NA.

Fragments are stored, and returned, in m/z order: mzLib’s writer sorts them. The table is a spectrum to plot as it is:

plot(ions$records$fragment_mz, ions$records$fragment_intensity, type = "h", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "m/z", ylab = "relative intensity", ylim = c(0, 1.1))
text(ions$records$fragment_mz, ions$records$fragment_intensity, ions$records$annotation,
     pos = 3, cex = 0.8)

A library has tens of fragment ions per precursor. For a whole library, write the table to disk with out (a .tsv) and read that with read.delim(), rather than returning it as one document.

Large libraries: index-only

mzLib opens a library one of two ways. Loaded whole, every precursor and every fragment is in memory. Index-only, the precursors are in memory and each precursor’s fragment block is read from disk when it is asked for. mzLib chooses by file size (MslFileTypeHandler.Open): a library at or above MslFileTypeHandler.DefaultIndexOnlyThresholdBytes, 1 GiB in the mzLib this bridge is built from, opens index-only. mzLibR sends nothing unless you pass index_only_threshold, a size in bytes; 0 opens every library index-only:

small <- library_read("synthetic_library.msl", index_only_threshold = 0, limit = 2)
small$is_index_only
#> [1] TRUE
small$index_only_threshold
#> [1] 0
small$records$full_sequence
#> [1] "PEPTIDEK" "KEDITPEP"

The rows are the same in both modes; only memory and speed differ. A compressed library (is_compressed) always loads whole: its fragment offsets point into the decompressed data, so mzLib decompresses it all and is_index_only stays FALSE whatever the threshold. And index-only with fragments reads every fragment block from disk twice, once to count the rows and once to write them; without fragments it reads no fragment block at all, which is the fast way to list the precursors of a very large library.

Many libraries at once

library_read_many() reads a list of libraries into one long table, in one bridge process. Its first two columns say where each row came from (source_index, 1-based, and source_path), and files has one row per library:

batch <- library_read_many(c("synthetic_library.msl", "myPrositLib.msl"))
batch
#> <mzlibr_library_batch> library read
#>   2 inputs: 2 read, 0 failed (on_error = "fail")
#>   11 rows in `records`, 11 records
batch$files$record_count
#> [1] 6 5
table(batch$records$source_index)
#> 
#> 1 2 
#> 6 5
batch$files$absent_fields
#> [[1]]
#> character(0)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "ion_mobility"      "protein_accession" "protein_name"     
#> [4] "gene_name"

threads reads that many libraries at once. The answer is identical at any value; the default is 1 because a library loaded whole is held in memory while its rows are written. on_error = "skip" records an unreadable library in its row of files and reads the rest. Never loop library_read() over files: each call starts a bridge process.

Traps

  • Stored order, not m/z order. Rows follow precursor_index. Sort on precursor_mz yourself.
  • The extra digits are the float. precursor_mz, retention_time and ion_mobility are stored as 32-bit floats and widened by mzLib, so 465.74 reads back as 465.739990234375. Round them for display; they carry no more precision than about seven significant digits.
  • nce is a whole number. The format stores NCE x 10 and mzLib reads it back with integer division, so an NCE of 27.5 reads as 27.
  • Converted libraries are thin. A library converted from .msp has no NCE, dissociation type, q-value, ion mobility or protein (see above).
  • A broken file is an error, not a short table. mzLib checks the whole file (magic number, version, footer, precursor count and a CRC-32 checksum) before it returns a single precursor. A damaged library raises mzlib_bridge_error with error_type "InvalidDataException", and a file that is not a library raises it with "FormatException". A file whose name does not end in .msl is an mzlib_usage_error before anything is opened.

What this does not do

  • Read a text library (.msp, pDeep, ms2pip). mzLib can turn one into a library in memory (MslConverter.FromMspFile), but no wire verb projects it yet.
  • Write a library. mzLib writes them (MslLibrary.Save); no wire verb projects that yet.
  • Query by m/z or retention-time window. mzLib’s QueryMzWindow and QueryWindow are what a search engine calls. To find a precursor here, read the table and filter it.

mzLib #1383 added the entrapment flag and made rt_is_calibrated work, #1421 added GetEntry without fragments, and #1420 made libraries over 2 GB open.
